newsitem.title: USA: Inland says it would consider a merger.
newsitem.headline: Inland says it would consider a merger.

text.p: A consolidation of the U.S. integrated steel industry "probably makes sense at this point in time" in order for prices paid by large contract customers to increase, said Inland Steel Industries Inc Chairman Bob Darnall on Monday.

"We have large customers with strong purchasing power and that is an influence on overall industry pricing," Darnall told reporters in a conference call after the release of Inland's first-quarter results. "That is one issue that probably speaks to industry consolidation...industry consolidation does probably make sense at this point in time."
Darnall declined to comment on whether his company is in talks with other steelmakers about merging some of their operations with Inland's.

Inland confirmed last week that it had discussions last year with USX-U.S. Steel Group about merging operations between the two companies. Inland said the talks broke off because the company decided it was not in the best interest of shareholders.
The confirmation came a few days after U.S. Steel President Paul Wilhelm said at an analysts' meeting that his company was scouting partners for mergers. He identified Inland as a potential partner.

At least half a dozen steelmakers supply a handful of large contract customers, including automakers. Those customers have been able to keep a lid on the prices they pay for steel because of the oversupply in the industry.
That in turn has dampened steel earnings because of the large amount of business they conduct with contract customers. In Inland's case, two-thirds of its steel is sold on a contract basis.
Several industry analysts said recently that steelmakers are moving toward a consolidation of the industry to give their companies more leverage in price negotiations with contract customers.

Darnall, while declining to be specific, said his company would consider merging its operations with another company. "I think rational people would see it as a way to strengthen the steel company," he said. "We would be willing to consider those kinds of things."

Separately, Inland reported earlier Monday first-quarter earnings of $0.59 per share versus $0.31 per share last year. This year's result was above Wall Street's consensus estimate of $0.43 per share.
Shares of Inland were up 1/8 to 18-1/2 in morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Darnall said the improved earnings were driven by reduced costs, improved yields from its operations, and the sale of more value-added products.
